The fog over the salt marsh does not lift so much as it thins, turning from milk to grease, until the black ribs of the old pilings show through like broken teeth. 

Every morning starts here, with this specific quality of gray. It is not an empty color; it is crowded with water, soot, brine, and the ghosts of ships that burned down to their waterlines sixty years before anyone thought to build a bridge. If you stand on the sill of the kitchen door with a cracked mug of chicory, you can hear the buoys before you see them. They don’t chime. They grope against their chains, clanking with the dull, rusted percussion of iron striking wet weed.

There is a superstition among the people who stay through the winter that if you leave an unlit lantern on your front stoop, the sea will think the house is already drowned and pass it by. No one admits to believing this, yet walking down the lane between the low-slung clapboard cottages, you will see a hurricane lamp on every third porch, dry-wicked, cold, dusted with salt-rime. It is an instinct older than theology: the desire to play dead until the weather changes its mind.

Inside the station, the barograph drum turns with the slow, indifferent dignity of a planet. Its brass arm holds an inked nib against gridded paper, dragging a purple line across the week. When the barometric pressure drops, the line falls like a bird hit with shot. When the air hardens into frost and the sky clears until it hurts to look up, the line creeps toward the upper margin, trembling whenever a logging truck grinds its gears three miles inland. 

I have watched that needle for eleven years. In that time, I have learned that the world does not want to be described; it wants to be tolerated. Most human misery comes from trying to impose a plot on a coastline. 

Take the tide, for instance. People from the cities come out in August with folding chairs and umbrellas the color of fruit rinds. They sit on the sandbars at two in the afternoon and marvel at how gentle the Atlantic is, how wide the apron of gray sand stretches before them. They do not look at the wrack line eighty yards behind their backs—the tangle of bladderwrack, plastic bottle caps, skate eggs, and dried skate wings that marks the real border. By five o'clock, the water has crept through the cut behind them, severed the sandbar from the dunes, and turned their picnic into an archipelago. Then comes the scrambling, the sodden canvas bags, the wet dogs, the indignation. They look at the water as if it has broken an agreement. But the water has no contract with August. It answers to a dead stone wheeling three hundred thousand kilometers overhead, pulling oceans across rocks like a boy dragging a sheet off an unmade bed.

In the back room behind the weather desk sits the cabinet of duplicate keys. It has forty-two hooks, though there are only nine houses left on the spit that still have roofs. The keys are heavy, cut from yellow brass or cold iron, labeled with masking tape that has yellowed to the color of earwax. Some of the tags say names: *Vance*, *O’Hagan*, *The Miller Girl*. Some say descriptions: *Shed with blue latch*, *Wellhouse*, *Pump under the elderberry*. 

If you take the keys off their hooks, they smell of grease and cedar shavings. Once a month, I walk the lane and try them in the deadbolts. Most slide in easily, bathed in WD-40, turning with a heavy, satisfying clunk that shakes the dry rot in the lintels. Inside, the houses smell identical: cold linoleum, mice, old newspapers, and that mineral sadness that lives in rooms where sunlight falls on wallpaper but touches no warm flesh.

In the Miller house, there is a calendar on the kitchen wall from 1984. The picture above the days is of a golden retriever holding a mallard in its mouth, soft-eyed, its coat wet from some midwestern pond. May 14th is circled in blue ballpoint. Beside it, written in a hand that must have been shaky even then, are two words: *Doctor said.* Nothing else. No verdict, no grief, no explanation. Just the boundary between before and after, pinned to a Tuesday forty years ago.

I stood there last week while the wind rattled the single-pane glass until the putty gave off a dry rattle like rice in a jar. I wondered what the doctor had said. Had he said six months? Had he said it was benign? Had he simply looked at an X-ray and sighed the way men do when they know they are the bearer of an unmanageable truth? It didn’t matter. May 14th had come, and then May 15th, and eventually the house had emptied out, and now the mold was eating the retriever from the tail forward.

People often ask what one does out here when the ferry stops running in November. The question reveals a misunderstanding of solitude. Silence is not an absence; it is a weight. It requires maintenance. 

You must keep the flue clean, or the birch smoke backs down the chimney and suffocates the geraniums on the sill. You must grease the pulleys on the wind generator, or the bearings seize during a gale, and you spend three weeks hauling car batteries to the general store on a rusted hand-truck. You must watch the edges of the marsh for the first skim of black ice, because once the ice locks the reeds together, the foxes can cross from the mainland, and then the feral cats go mad in the underbrush, screaming like discarded instruments in the dark.

There is plenty to do. You do not think about your life, which is a mercy. When you live among many people, you are constantly reminded of the shape of yourself, because you are always bumping against the shapes of others—their ambitions, their divorces, the shoes they choose to wear to the bakery. You see your reflection in the glass of storefronts, in the irritation of clerks, in the polite distance people keep on the train. 

Out here, there are no mirrors except the tide pools when the wind dies at dusk. And if you look into a tide pool, you do not see yourself; you see limpets, barnacles, the brown ribbon of kelp swaying in the undertow, and, behind them, an enormous and entirely indifferent sky. 

The barograph needle clicks. A drop of purple ink falls onto the paper. It is noon. The fog is finally gone, replaced by a light so sharp and cold that the dunes look carved from suet. Two gulls sit on the beacon post, shoulders hunched against the northern draft, waiting for something small to die in the grass. I put the kettle on the iron stove. The metal groans as the heat finds it, expanding molecule by molecule, settling into its work.
